slot.brief: For a simple one-electron or two-electron half-cell (e.g. metal ion concentration given at 298 K), compute the electrode potential using the Nernst equation; straightforward plug-in.

stem: What is the reduction potential of a copper electrode dipped in a $0.01\ \text{M}\ \text{Cu}^{2+}$ solution at $298\ \text{K}$? (Given: $E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}} = +0.34\ \text{V}$ and $\dfrac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059\ \text{V}$)
working:
The half-cell reduction reaction is:
$$\text{Cu}^{2+}(aq) + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}(s)$$

Here, the number of electrons transferred is $n = 2$.

Applying the Nernst equation at $298\ \text{K}$:
$$E = E^\circ - \dfrac{0.059}{n}\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{1}{[\text{Cu}^{2+}]}\right)$$

Substitute the given values:
$$E = 0.34 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{1}{0.01}\right)$$
$$E = 0.34 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log_{10}(10^2)$$
$$E = 0.34 - \dfrac{0.059}{2} \times 2$$
$$E = 0.34 - 0.059 = +0.281\ \text{V}$$

Independent check: Nernst: E = E° + (0.059/n) log[Cu²⁺] with n = 2. log(0.01) = −2, so E = 0.34 + (0.059/2)(−2) = 0.34 − 0.059 = +0.281 V.

Option A encodes calculating the oxidation potential ($E_{\text{ox}} = -E_{\text{red}} = -0.281\ \text{V}$) instead of the reduction potential.
Option B encodes forgetting that $n = 2$ and dividing by $n = 1$, yielding $0.34 - 0.118 = +0.222\ \text{V}$.
